## Looking back on the module

This module turned out to be one of the most **practically useful**
parts of my MSc so far. Going in, I thought a "portfolio module" would
be lightweight - something to polish a CV. Coming out, I realise how
much of what we covered maps directly onto **how real corporate teams
actually work**: version control, reproducible reporting, personal
branding, and professional web presence.

The sessions were consistently engaging, and the **guest lectures were
a highlight throughout**. Hearing practitioners speak on **data, AI
usage, and business analytics in industry** gave context that no
textbook could match - it made the tools we were learning feel
immediately relevant.

## Why this module matters in the corporate world

Much of what we learned - **Git, GitHub, Quarto, web development
fundamentals** - is not optional in modern workplaces. It's expected.

- **Git and GitHub** are the universal language of collaborative work,
  not just for developers but increasingly for analysts, data
  scientists, and business teams who track configuration or
  documentation under version control.
- **Quarto** bridges a gap I didn't realise existed: the gap between an
  analyst's Jupyter notebook and a stakeholder-ready report. In
  industry, *"send me the analysis"* means a clean, reproducible
  document - not a raw notebook.
- **Web development fundamentals** - HTML, CSS, SCSS, site
  configuration - are table-stakes for anyone who wants to publish
  their work or build internal tools.

Taken together, this module gave me a **toolkit I can walk into any
corporate environment with** and be immediately productive.

## Guest lectures - data, AI, and business analytics

The guest lectures were genuinely one of the best parts of the module.
Speakers covered **how data and AI are being used across industry**, and
how **business analytics is shaping decision-making** in real
organisations.

A few takeaways that stuck with me:

- **AI in analytics isn't replacing analysts - it's amplifying them.**
  The speakers were consistent on this: LLMs and automated tooling
  handle the grunt work, but framing the right question, sanity-checking
  results, and communicating insight still needs a human in the loop.
- **Data literacy is a business skill**, not a technical one. The most
  valuable analysts translate between data teams and commercial
  stakeholders - and that translation work is something no AI tool
  replaces yet.
- **Portfolios matter in hiring.** More than one speaker mentioned that
  a clean GitHub and a public project page shortcut entire interview
  rounds. A working site *is* evidence.
- **Reproducibility is competitive advantage.** Teams that can rerun
  last quarter's analysis with one command move faster than teams that
  can't find last quarter's spreadsheet.

Those sessions reframed how I think about my own trajectory. The
transition from full-stack engineering into business analytics isn't a
side-step - it's an expansion. The tools are familiar; the audience is
new.

## Skills I built

### Git and GitHub

I've used Git before in team settings, but this module made me take
**solo Git discipline** seriously for the first time. Writing small,
descriptive commits; maintaining a clean `.gitignore`; deploying through
GitHub Pages rather than uploading files manually - these habits sound
small but they separate amateur work from professional work.

### Quarto

Easily the biggest new skill. Before this module, my idea of a
"portfolio" was a static HTML page or a LinkedIn profile. Quarto turned
it into something far more powerful: a **living, executable document**
where every chart regenerates from code, every page is version
controlled, and the entire site is reproducible on any machine.

### Web development

SCSS variables, Google Fonts, Bootswatch themes, favicons, navbar
configuration - none of this was in my day-to-day before. Getting
hands-on with a real site (rather than reading about CSS) made the
concepts stick in a way passive learning never does.

### Writing for a broader audience

Writing the project pages and this reflection pushed me to **frame
technical work for readers who aren't deep in the details**. That's a
core communication skill in any analytics role - the audience is
usually a business stakeholder, not a fellow engineer.

## Challenges I overcame

::: {.callout-warning title="The friction points"}
- **YAML indentation.** `_quarto.yml` doesn't forgive mistakes, and my
  first silent-failing navbar cost me an hour. Lesson: validate
  incrementally.
- **GitHub Pages + Jekyll.** Forgetting `.nojekyll` led to a confused
  evening of *"why is my CSS missing?"*. Trivial fix once I knew where
  to look.
- **Balancing polish and substance.** It's tempting to spend a whole
  day on colour palettes. I set myself a rule: **content first, styling
  last**.
:::

## What this means for my career

Three lessons I'm taking directly into the next chapter:

1. **Reproducibility as a default.** Every analysis under version
   control, every chart regenerated from code, every decision traceable
   to the data it came from.
2. **Public presence matters.** A polished portfolio and a clean GitHub
   profile do a lot of the hiring conversation for you, before you're
   even in the room.
3. **Communication is half the work.** Technical depth alone doesn't
   win roles - being able to explain what you did, and why, in clear
   writing, is what gets remembered.

## What I'd do differently

1. **Start the commit discipline from day one** rather than catching up
   mid-project.
2. **Engage with the guest lectures even more actively** - ask more
   questions, follow up with the speakers afterwards.
3. **Treat the portfolio as a long-term asset** from the start, not a
   submission to rush at the end.

## Next steps

- Add a **third analytics project** using a real public dataset.
- Wire up **GitHub Actions** to auto-deploy on every push.
- Keep the site **updated quarterly** as coursework and experience
  grow.
